title: Hummerret (Lobster Dish)
description: Prepared with lobster, salad oil, and bread.
steps: Choose a medium-sized lobster, not too large.
Put a handful of salt in a pot of boiling water and after having tied the claws together, fasten the lobster to the water.
Cook for half an hour to an hour, depending on its size.
When it is done, take it up and lay it with the back up on a sieve to dry.
When it is cold, scrape the body and tail and the claws.
Boil the lobster and pick out the meat, being careful that the shell remains intact.
Rub the shell with salad oil; into as much of the red roe as you have, add a little nutmeg, cayenne pepper, lemon juice, butter and a little egg yolk.
If it is lobster, rub the shell with egg yolk.
Put the meat back into the shells, cover lightly with soft bread and butter and bake brown in the oven.
Arrange with parsley and lemon slices around it.

title: Hvost (Quinces)

ingredients.name: Sugar (1 pound sugar per 1 pound quinces)

steps: Put the quinces in boiling water and cook until they begin to soften.
Remove them, peel them, and cut them according to their size into 4 or 8 pieces.
Remove the core and all the stone around them, and weigh them.

For 1 pound of quinces take 1 pound of sugar, which is put on the stove with 1 pint of water; when the first scum is removed, put in the quinces, stir well, cook evenly for half an hour or longer, if needed, so that they can become perfectly tender and the syrup even.
Store them, cover a cloth over and the next day they are covered with paper, dipped in brandy, and tied.

title: Hvost-Marmelade (Quince Marmalade)
description: A fruit preserve made with quince, quinces, and water.

ingredients.name: Sugar (1 pound sugar per 1 pound quinces)

steps: Dry the quinces, cut the peelings and weigh them.
For 1 pound of peelings take 1 pint of water, which they cook very gently for one hour, after which they are strained.
Slice the quinces in 4 to 8 pieces, remove the core and all the stone, weigh them.

For 1 pound of quinces take 1 pound of sugar, which is put in the water that has been strained from the peelings; when it is melted, put the quinces in and cook with the lid on, over a good and even fire, only not quickly, and with constant stirring, until they are tender.
This can take a couple of hours.
During this slow cooking, under a closed lid, the quinces often become red; if not, you can add currant juice.
When reduced to a soft pulp, stir in almost 1 pound of sugar for each pound of fruit; cook for another 10 minutes, stirring.
Remove from heat, and when cold, put into small jars or glasses with brandy paper over.

title: Håndfager (Hand-Baked Pancakes)
description: Prepared with butter, milk, and salt.
steps: Heat butter on a griddle for the first pancakes

The griddle must be hot before you begin baking and butter is added to the griddle for the first pancakes, later not. The dough is held thin on the griddle and when the underside is baked enough, the pancake is turned. This is best done by loosening it around the edge with a knife, taking it at two spots at the edge and turning it quickly, after which it is baked finished on the other side

For the pancakes to become hard, they must be baked slowly over the griddle, not burning, as this gives too harsh heat, from which the pancakes become dark and not good; these should not be laid warm on top of one another. If you wish the pancakes soft, little butter is added to the griddle for each pancake, they are baked faster and laid warm on top of one another
If the dough becomes too thick during baking, it can be thinned with a little milk
The first pancakes are seldom whole, but when several are baked on the griddle, it goes better

title: Hønesuppe (Chicken Soup) [Especially Recommended]
description: A soup made with chicken, water, and salt.

title: Kantucci af Rækkehøn (Stuffed Duck Shoulder)
description: Prepared with breadcrumbs, egg yolks, and vegetables.
steps: Take a 4 pound shoulder that should not be crushed at the butcher, wash it and lay it on the board with the inner part facing up.
Cut out the shoulder blood and boil it to make it completely clean.

Then cut out with a sharp, pointed knife the meat along the lower edge of the bone and the hallobone from the other, being careful to remove the hallobone between the first and second rib and be careful not to break the meat or cut through the bone.
Shape the end of the bone so it resembles a duck leg.

Fill the shoulder with one or another forcemeat or stuffing, though the most commonly used is prepared as follows: boil eggs, scrape them and cook them in three different ways; dissolve breadcrumbs in lukewarm water and strain in a clean cloth.
When the eggs are soft, which should take about half an hour, let them cool and mix together with the breadcrumbs, with a bit of butter, two egg yolks and a little salt and pepper.
After it is stuffed in the meat, bind it together so it resembles a duck.
Place it in a roasting pan on some slices of vegetables and roast in a hot oven for approximately 20 minutes per pound.
Meanwhile prepare root vegetables and parsnip root vegetables by cutting them into small pieces, cook them tender in broth and salted water, and place them in cold water to preserve their color.
When the roast is done, take it up on a warm platter and keep it warm without drying while the sauce is prepared.

The sauce is prepared from browned butter with a little flour, upon which the broth from the roasting pan is poured from the vegetables into the sauce, and finally a spoonful of raw egg yolk and a little powdered sugar are stirred in.
Warm the vegetables in the sauce and arrange them around the meat.
The shoulder blade should be scraped after being cooked and have the broad end attached so it resembles feathers, then placed in the sauce beside the roast, which is then served.

title: Mælkemad (Milk Porridge)
description: Prepared with milk, grains or rice, and water.
steps: In the preparation of porridge, one must ensure that it boils gently, not fiercely, and without interruption.

For milk porridge, place a thick sheet iron in the bottom of the porridge pot, and if the cooking boils over and you must place stronger fire underneath, loosen this sheet, whereby the porridge cooks easily.
Over an open fire one can scarcely cook milk porridge.

If it is a thin pair of pots you must cook in, it is all the more inclined to scorch, and you must then smear it inside with soft butter and cover it with water; a good remedy against getting milk porridge scorched is to put a little prepared soda in the milk when it is put over the fire.
It gives absolutely no taste; about a teaspoon is enough for 3 pints milk.
The milk must always boil before the grains are added, and the porridge should not be thinned during cooking; hereby it scorches easily.
Rice porridge becomes best when you do not stir it, but then you must never neglect to smear the porridge first.
When the milk or water is in a hard boil, the grains are added by the side where it boils strongest and the lid is laid on.

The fire must be watched with great care, so that toward the end of cooking it will stand almost still 15 minutes or so before serving, stir in the porridge, and you shall have absolutely no fear, if it seems thin; for by boiling the last quarter under constant stirring, it will become proper.
Once you have stirred in the porridge, it must be done regularly.
In no kind of milk porridge is salt added before it is taken from the fire.

For every quart of milk, take a little heaping tablespoon of cornstarch or groats, which is stirred in some of the cold milk; the remainder is put on the fire, and when it boils, the meal is stirred in, and it boils until the milk is thickened.

Two egg yolks are stirred with cold sugar, thinned with warm milk, and poured into the porridge and stirred until it begins to boil; then it is poured into the tureen in which is a little salt and a couple drops vanilla; it tastes good instead of vanilla to boil a couple sticks of hot cinnamon in the milk.
You can place boiled eggs cut in half in the tureen; in the milk in which they boil, there must be sugar and a little cinnamon.
This milk is then strained and added to the remaining milk.
The soup is eaten with small rusks or baked bread, and one usually reckons a quart of milk for 3 persons.

title: Salt Walnuts for Winter

title: Stegt Høns (Roasted Chicken)

steps: As soon as the chicken is slaughtered and cold, have a pot full of boiling water ready.

Cut the birds in the following manner: cut a slit along the backbone and pull it out boneless, and large enough that a hand can pass through it, and remove the contents.
Remove the crop, which lies at the bird's gullet boundary.

The entire cleaning is done in lukewarm water and must be very careful; in the next water add a piece of soda; let cold water run through the bird many times, and when you are completely certain of the cleaning, dry it well inside with a clean cloth.
The head and bones below the ankle are cut off and not used.
The gizzard, heart and liver, when cleaned, can be used in various ways; either minced and added to the filling or in the sauce, or one can simply put them inside the whole bird.
On hens and chickens the breastbone can be cut inside to give them a round shape, but on game birds it must be done from the outside.
One can have a bread dough and stick it between the loose skin and the meat; it gives the breast a beautiful golden appearance.

To prevent the bones from sticking out when the bird is cooked, you can cut a hole fairly high up on each side of the cut skin, push the hairs back so that the tendons can be pulled into the hole and tied around them.
On ducks and geese the breastbone is not cut.
One should never use a fork to turn the birds—because precious juice runs out—but use a clean wooden spoon.
One counts generally 15 minutes of roasting for every pound the bird weighs.
Wash the game bird in cold water.
If you prefer, you can singe it.
To fill it around where the crop has been; for this use is allowed a piece of a few ounces of white bread that is soaked in milk and then stands covered for an hour.
A piece of cold butter is stirred until smooth, then the bread is stirred, after being moistened into pieces with a spoon, salt, a little sweet ginger, a pair of cloves and 3 eggs.

When it is well mixed, one can add the gizzard, liver and heart, which are finely minced, fill it in the skin and sew it, but the filling must not push down into the game bird, so a piece of white bread must be placed in the internal hole below the neck.
The oven must be well heated before the game bird is put in, and it must have an even warmth, but not too strong, as it would otherwise become too dark brown.
It cannot be roasted in a pot when it is filled.
It is placed in with water and a little salt, by which it is gradually basted; later butter is laid on it, by which it is then basted.
The best filling for a duck is apples and good prunes, it gives the most pleasant flavor; but others allow a dough of eggs, bread and milk and fill with it.
One can also just rub it inside with salt and pepper and then place a piece of juniper wood inside; these are completely consumed during roasting, but they give the duck a fresh flavor.
It is placed in the oven with a little water on it, which soon becomes fat, by which the duck is often basted.
As sauce sharp red wine sauce can be used, but generally only sauce made in the usual way is used.
Fat should be well skimmed off before the sauce is made.

title: Ghyuldj Baladivessi
description: Prepared with starch, rose-water, and clotted cream.

ingredients.name: about a pound of wheat starch

steps: Put in a basin the whites of twenty eggs, and whip them up well
Add about a pound of wheat starch by degrees, stir it well, and mix it well with water, to form a very thin batter

Put over a charcoal fire a circular and slightly-domed sheet-iron, the under side in the centre of which you have previously cemented with ashes half an inch thick, to prevent it from getting fiercely hot

Cover it with the other half of the cakes, sprinkling rose-water and milk between each one as before
Put in a stewpan a pound of loaf sugar, with two pints of water, and set it to boil until it becomes a syrup
Take it off and pour it over the cakes, till covered, and let it remain covered until cold
Cut it up in diamonds, dish up and serve. Pounded almonds or pistachios may be used, if clotted cream is not handy
